recent_posts.title: Restoring a 1990s Ascend MAX 6000 ISP terminal server after 20 years
recent_posts.summary: A detailed restoration story of an Ascend MAX 6000 terminal server from the late 1990s, the kind of hardware that powered major ISPs like AOL. The unit had been sitting unused for over 20 years with no modem cards installed and a faulty power supply. The repair involved diagnosing a shorted DC/DC converter module (Vicor VI-J61), sourcing a replacement on eBay, modifying it to fit, and soldering it back in. After getting the hardware running, the team tackled the notoriously confusing Ascend configuration interface to set up PRI, PPP, and IP addressing for dial-in users. After hours of troubleshooting firmware compatibility issues with a V34 modem card and navigating cryptic menus, they successfully got a 56K dial-in connection working and reached the internet.

recent_posts.title: How curl went from a 12-line IRC bot helper to software running on Mars
recent_posts.summary: The origin story of curl, one of the most widely deployed pieces of software on Earth (and Mars). Daniel Stenberg, a Swedish developer from the Commodore 64 demo scene, built an IRC bot called Dancer in the mid-1990s that needed daily currency exchange rates. To fetch them, he adopted a 12-line C tool called httpget, fixed it, and eventually renamed it curl in March 1998. The libcurl library followed in 2001, and PHP's adoption of it as its default HTTP transfer layer triggered an explosion in usage. Today curl supports 28 URL schemes, has over 20 billion installations, runs on NASA's Ingenuity helicopter on Mars, and has 3,500+ contributors. The piece also covers curl's rigorous CVE-documentation security policy, the shutdown of its bug bounty program due to AI-generated fake reports, and a hands-on attempt to revive the original Dancer IRC bot from a 2002 SourceForge archive.

recent_posts.title: How VocalTech created the first commercial internet phone in 1995
recent_posts.summary: VoIP technology emerged from 1970s ARPANET experiments addressing packet network challenges like jitter and latency. Danny Cohen developed the Network Voice Protocol in 1974, leading to TCP/IP protocol separation. In 1995, Israeli startup VocalTech launched Internet Phone, the first commercial VoIP application enabling free long-distance calls over dial-up connections. Their dynamic jitter buffer innovation and IRC-based directory service revolutionized digital communication, spawning the modern VoIP industry and influencing platforms like Skype and Zoom.

recent_posts.title: Upgrading our ISP with ISDN
recent_posts.summary: ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network) provided fully digital telephone connections in the 1990s, offering 128 Kbps bandwidth by bonding two 64KB B channels using multilink PPP. Setting up an ISDN lab environment requires simulating telco infrastructure with equipment like the Adran Atlas 550, configuring terminal adapters, and establishing PRI connections. The setup demonstrates ISDN's key advantage: significantly lower latency (45ms vs 200ms) compared to analog dialup, despite modest download speeds. The implementation involves complex configurations including switch types, SPIDs, and various interface standards (U, S/T, NT1).

recent_posts.title: Dial-up Internet with 12 MODEMS
recent_posts.summary: An experimental project demonstrating multilink PPP technology by bonding 12 dial-up modems together to achieve broadband speeds. The team progressively scaled from 2 to 12 modems, troubleshooting hardware issues like dip switch configurations and finicky telephone jacks along the way. They successfully reached over 200 Kbps with 5 modems and ultimately 668 Kbps with all 12 modems connected, culminating in streaming YouTube over the combined dial-up connections.

recent_posts.title: 1995: The Year of the Virtual LAN
recent_posts.summary: Virtual LANs (VLANs) emerged in the late 1980s and early 1990s to solve network scalability and broadcast domain segmentation challenges. The technology evolved from early implementations like Alantec's bridge groups in 1989 through various proprietary solutions from vendors like Cisco, Kalpana, and Ungermann-Bass. After years of competing standards and interoperability issues, the IEEE 802.1Q standard was finalized in 1998, establishing the frame tagging method still used today. VLANs enable network administrators to create logical network separations on physical infrastructure, reducing broadcast traffic, improving security through isolation, and simplifying network management.

recent_posts.title: Pushing Dial-up Modems Further Than We EVER Thought Possible
Celebrating 30 years of Windows 95 with dial up internet connection
recent_posts.summary: A nostalgic look back at Windows 95's 30th anniversary, exploring its revolutionary features like the Start button, plug-and-play hardware support, native TCP/IP networking stack, and long filename support. The authors demonstrate connecting to the internet via dial-up modem on an original Windows 95 system, highlighting how the OS simplified internet access compared to Windows 3.1's complex third-party networking solutions. They discuss Windows 95's impact on internet adoption and reminisce about early web browsing, IRC, and the simpler computing era of the mid-1990s.

recent_posts.title: AfriNIC faces governance crisis threatening Africa's IP address system
recent_posts.summary: AfriNIC, Africa's regional internet registry responsible for IP address allocation, faces a governance crisis following suspended board elections due to allegations of vote tampering and forged proxies. ICANN has issued warnings demanding explanations and legitimate elections, threatening formal compliance review that could strip AfriNIC's accreditation. The crisis stems from years of legal battles, including a 2021 lawsuit that froze the registry's accounts and left it without leadership, potentially jeopardizing Africa's entire IP address infrastructure.

recent_posts.title: BBSing and the Demo Scene
recent_posts.summary: Explores the fascinating world of bulletin board systems (BBS) and the demo scene, where programmers created impressive 32KB programs featuring hour-long visual displays that captivated early computer enthusiasts.
